summary: Paul strengthens communities through Macedonia and Greece, reverses course when a plot threatens his voyage, and travels with a named multi-regional team. At Troas the believers gather on the first day of the week to break bread; Paul's long night teaching ends when Eutychus falls from a third-story window, but Paul embraces him and he is found alive. Hurrying past Ephesus, Paul summons its elders to Miletus for a farewell. He recalls humble, tearful, public and house-to-house ministry, testifies to the gospel of grace, anticipates bonds, declares his innocence, charges Spirit-appointed overseers to shepherd God's flock against wolves, commends them to God and the word, and points to his manual labor and care for the weak.
whyItMatters: Acts' fullest leadership speech measures ministry by presence, truth, tears, courage, work, and protection of vulnerable people rather than platform or profit. Paul does not idealize himself as invulnerable; he expects suffering and warns that danger can arise from within leadership itself. The community's grief shows authority held in accountable relationship, not detached office.

context.author: The Luke–Acts narrator presenting Paul's last movement through the Aegean and farewell to Ephesian leaders
context.audience: Communities and leaders inheriting responsibility after an apostolic founder departs
context.setting: Macedonia, Greece, Troas, the Aegean coast, and Miletus
context.literaryForm: Travel itinerary, meeting-and-restoration story, and testament-style farewell speech

outline.heading: A diverse team accompanies Paul's return through Macedonia
Eutychus falls during the Troas gathering and is restored
Paul travels to Miletus and rehearses his ministry
Elders are charged to guard the flock, work, give, and remember

keyVerses.text: But these things don’t count; nor do I hold my life dear to myself, so that I may finish my race with joy, and the ministry which I received from the Lord Jesus, to fully testify to the Good News of the grace of God.
keyVerses.why: Paul interprets his uncertain future through a received ministry of witness rather than self-preservation.

keyVerses.text: Take heed, therefore, to yourselves and to all the flock, in which the Holy Spirit has made you overseers, to shepherd the assembly of the Lord and God which he purchased with his own blood.
keyVerses.why: Leadership begins with self-watch, attends the whole flock, and protects people whose value comes from God's costly claim.

keyVerses.text: In all things I gave you an example, that so laboring you ought to help the weak, and to remember the words of the Lord Jesus, that he himself said, ‘It is more blessed to give than to receive.’ ”
keyVerses.why: A saying not preserved in the Gospels grounds leadership in work and generous support for the weak.

questions.question: Why does Luke list so many travel companions?
questions.answer: Sopater, Aristarchus, Secundus, Gaius, Timothy, Tychicus, and Trophimus represent several regions touched by the mission. They may be delegates associated with a collection for Jerusalem, though Acts does not state that here. The list makes the journey accountable and communal rather than Paul's private enterprise.

questions.question: Does ‘the first day of the week’ prove a complete Sunday worship pattern?
questions.answer: The believers gather to break bread on the first day and Paul teaches into the night, early evidence for first-day Christian assembly. Ancient reckoning can place the evening at the start or end of the day, and ‘breaking bread’ can include communal meal and Eucharistic resonance. One scene supports the pattern without describing a full universal liturgy.

questions.question: Was Eutychus dead or only unconscious?
questions.answer: Luke says he was taken up dead, while Paul says, ‘his life is in him’; after the embrace the community brings him alive and is greatly comforted. The narrative intends a life-restoring event, though interpreters debate whether Paul's words announce reversal or correct a mistaken diagnosis. The emphasis is recovered life and communal consolation, not blaming a tired listener.

questions.question: Why does Paul speak to elders but call them overseers who shepherd?
questions.answer: The same group is called presbyteroi, elders, in verse 17; Paul says the Spirit made them episkopoi, overseers, and commands them poimainein, to shepherd. The terms overlap here before later church traditions develop more fixed distinctions among offices. Whatever polity is inferred, vigilance and care define the role.

questions.question: What does Paul mean by teaching ‘publicly and from house to house’?
questions.answer: He recalls ministry in civic or communal settings and in households, with Jews and Greeks alike, centered on repentance toward God and faith toward Jesus. The phrase describes range and personal presence; it is not necessarily a command for one modern evangelism method. Tears and trials make the recollection relational rather than statistical.

questions.question: How can the Spirit both compel Paul and warn him of bonds?
questions.answer: Paul is ‘bound in the spirit’ toward Jerusalem while the Holy Spirit testifies in city after city that imprisonment and affliction await. Guidance does not mean avoidance of hardship; warning prepares him to enter it knowingly. The text leaves some ambiguity between Paul's inward resolve and the Holy Spirit's testimony, which chapter 21 intensifies.

questions.question: Why do manuscripts differ in verse 28?
questions.answer: Important witnesses read ‘the church of God, which he purchased with his own blood’; others read ‘the church of the Lord,’ and combinations such as the WEB's ‘Lord and God’ reflect the difficult transmission. ‘God's own blood’ is the harder, striking reading and may mean the blood of his own Son. The variant affects wording used in christological argument, not the charge to care for a costly flock.

questions.question: Who are the ‘savage wolves’?
questions.answer: Paul warns of destructive teachers entering from outside and of men arising from among the elders who distort truth to draw disciples after themselves. Threat is not ethnicized and cannot be projected onto Jews or Gentiles as groups; it is diagnosed by exploitative teaching and self-centered following. Leaders must first watch themselves.

questions.question: Where is ‘more blessed to give than receive’ in the Gospels?
questions.answer: No canonical Gospel preserves this saying, so Acts witnesses to remembered Jesus tradition beyond the written Gospel quotations. Paul links it to his own manual work, freedom from coveting wealth, and support for weak people. The saying is not contempt for receiving needed care; it directs those with strength and resources toward generosity.

glossary.def: Overlapping leadership descriptions in this speech; the leaders are charged to shepherd rather than exploit.
A farewell address in which a departing leader reviews conduct, warns of danger, and commissions successors.
A coastal city south of Ephesus where Paul summons the Ephesian elders.
